title: Telling Time: From Sundials to Atomic Clocks
summary: How people measured time through history, from the Sun and sundials to water clocks, hourglasses, gear and pendulum clocks, and today's atomic clocks.
poll: The invention of clocks changed people's lives more than the invention of the phone.

versions.title: Clocks Long Ago
versions.text:
What time is it? Look at a clock. But long ago, there were no clocks.

So they used the Sun. Was the Sun high? Then it was noon. Did the Sun go down? Then it was night.

Then came the sundial. It has a stick. The Sun hits the stick. The stick casts a shadow. The shadow moves as the Sun moves. Lines show the time. Sundials were used in Egypt. That was more than 3,000 years ago!

But a sundial did not work at night. It did not work on a gray day.

So they made clocks with water. Drops fell out of a pot. Less water meant more time. A man named al-Jazari made a big one. It was shaped like an elephant!

Some used an hourglass. Sand fell from the top to the bottom. Ships took them to sea.

Then came clocks with gears. Gears are wheels with teeth. They turn the hands of a clock.

Now we have atomic clocks. They count tiny bits called atoms. They are the best. Your phone gets its time from them!

versions.title: Clocks Long Ago
versions.text:
What time is it? Today, you can look at a clock or a phone. But long ago, there were no clocks at all.

People used the Sun to tell time. When the Sun was high, it was the middle of the day. When the Sun set, the day was done.

Then people made the sundial. A sundial has a stick that sticks up. The Sun makes it cast a shadow. As the Sun moves, the shadow moves too. Marks show the hours. People in Egypt used sundials more than 3,000 years ago.

But a sundial has a problem. It does not work at night or on a cloudy day.

So people made water clocks. Water dripped out of a pot. The less water was left, the more time had passed. About 800 years ago, a man named al-Jazari built a huge water clock. It looked like an elephant!

Some people used an hourglass. Sand fell from the top part to the bottom part. Sailors used them on ships.

Later, people built clocks with gears. Gears are wheels with teeth. They turn the hands of a clock.

Today, we have atomic clocks. They count the tiny moves of atoms. They are the best clocks of all. Your phone gets its time from them!

versions.title: Telling Time: From Sundials to Atomic Clocks
versions.text:
Whenever you want to know the time today, you can simply glance at a clock or a phone. For most of human history, however, people had no mechanical clocks and depended on observing nature.

Ancient communities relied on the movement of the Sun. They knew that midday had arrived when the Sun reached its highest point, and that the day had ended when it disappeared below the horizon.

Eventually, people invented the sundial, an instrument with an upright stick or pointer. Its shadow moves gradually across markings that show the hours as the Sun travels across the sky. Communities in ancient Egypt were using sundials more than 3,000 years ago. However, these devices were useless at night or under cloudy skies, since they depended on sunlight.

To solve this problem, people developed water clocks, in which water dripped from a container at a steady rate, so the falling water level showed how much time had passed. About 800 years ago, the brilliant engineer al-Jazari built a celebrated water clock shaped like an elephant. Other people measured shorter periods with marked candles or with sand-filled hourglasses, which sailors carried on long voyages.

Roughly 700 years ago, Europeans built the earliest mechanical clocks, which used falling weights and gears, toothed wheels that turn one another, to move the hands. Unfortunately, these early machines were not very accurate, and some gained or lost many minutes every day.

In 1656, the Dutch scientist Christiaan Huygens designed a clock controlled by a pendulum, a hanging weight that swings back and forth with a steady rhythm. His invention was far more accurate than earlier clocks. Centuries later, in the 1920s, engineers developed quartz clocks, which contain a tiny crystal that can vibrate thousands of times every second when electricity passes through it.

Today, scientists rely on atomic clocks. The first practical one was completed in 1955. These clocks measure time by counting the extremely regular vibrations of atoms. They are the most accurate timekeepers ever invented, because the best of them would not gain or lose a single second over millions of years. Navigation satellites carry atomic clocks, which help them synchronize the time on your phone with clocks around the world.

versions.title: Telling Time: From Sundials to Atomic Clocks
versions.text:
Whenever you want to know the time today, you can simply glance at a clock or a phone. Throughout most of human history, however, people possessed no mechanical timekeeping devices whatsoever and depended on observing their natural surroundings.

Ancient communities relied on the apparent movement of the Sun, recognizing that midday had arrived when the Sun reached its highest position and that the day had concluded when it disappeared below the horizon.

Eventually, people invented the sundial, an instrument consisting of a vertical stick or pointer whose shadow travels gradually across markings that indicate the hours as the Sun moves across the sky. Communities in ancient Egypt were using sundials more than 3,000 years ago. Nevertheless, these devices were useless at night or under cloudy skies, since they depended completely on sunlight.

To overcome this limitation, people developed water clocks, in which water dripped from a container at a consistent rate. The declining water level revealed how much time had elapsed. Approximately 800 years ago, the brilliant engineer al-Jazari constructed a celebrated water clock shaped like an elephant, while other people measured shorter intervals with marked candles or with sand-filled hourglasses, which sailors carried on lengthy voyages.

Roughly 700 years ago, Europeans constructed the earliest mechanical clocks, which relied on falling weights and interlocking gears, toothed wheels that rotate one another, to advance the hands. Unfortunately, these early machines were not particularly precise, and some gained or lost many minutes every day.

In 1656, the Dutch scientist Christiaan Huygens designed a clock regulated by a pendulum, a suspended weight that swings back and forth with a remarkably consistent rhythm. His invention was dramatically more precise than earlier clocks. Centuries later, during the 1920s, engineers developed quartz clocks, which contain a tiny crystal that can vibrate thousands of times every second when electricity passes through it.

Contemporary scientists rely on atomic clocks, the first practical example of which was completed in 1955, and which measure time by counting the extraordinarily regular vibrations of atoms. These instruments are the most precise timekeepers ever invented, because the best of them would neither gain nor lose a single second over millions of years. Navigation satellites carry atomic clocks, which enable them to synchronize the time on your phone with clocks throughout the world, an accomplishment that would certainly have astonished the ancient Egyptians.

versions.title: Telling Time: From Sundials to Atomic Clocks
versions.text:
Whenever you want to know the time today, you can simply glance at a clock or a phone, but throughout most of human history, people possessed no mechanical timekeeping devices whatsoever and depended entirely on observing their natural surroundings.

Ancient communities relied on the apparent movement of the Sun, recognizing that midday had arrived when the Sun reached its highest position and that the day had concluded when it disappeared below the horizon.

Eventually, people invented the sundial, an instrument consisting of a vertical stick or pointer whose shadow travels gradually across markings that indicate the hours as the Sun moves across the sky. Communities in ancient Egypt were using sundials more than 3,000 years ago; nevertheless, these devices were useless at night or under cloudy skies, since they depended completely on direct sunlight.

To overcome this limitation, people developed water clocks, in which water dripped from a container at a consistent rate, so that the declining water level revealed how much time had elapsed. Approximately 800 years ago, the brilliant engineer al-Jazari, whose detailed descriptions of ingenious machines are still studied today, constructed a celebrated water clock shaped like an elephant. Other people measured shorter intervals with marked candles or with sand-filled hourglasses, which sailors carried on lengthy ocean voyages.

Roughly 700 years ago, Europeans constructed the earliest mechanical clocks, which relied on falling weights and interlocking gears, toothed wheels that rotate one another, to advance the hands. Unfortunately, these early machines were not particularly precise, and some gained or lost a considerable number of minutes every day.

In 1656, the Dutch scientist Christiaan Huygens designed a clock regulated by a pendulum, a suspended weight that swings back and forth with a remarkably consistent rhythm. His invention was dramatically more precise than any previous mechanical clock. Centuries later, during the 1920s, engineers developed quartz clocks, which contain a minuscule crystal that can vibrate thousands of times every second when electricity passes through it. Inexpensive quartz watches eventually became extraordinarily common.

Contemporary scientists rely on atomic clocks, the first practical example of which was completed in 1955, and which measure time by counting the extraordinarily regular vibrations of atoms. These instruments are the most precise timekeepers ever invented. The reason is that the best of them would neither gain nor lose a single second over millions of years. Navigation satellites orbiting Earth carry atomic clocks, which enable them to synchronize the time displayed on your phone with clocks throughout the world, an accomplishment that would certainly have astonished the ancient Egyptians who first followed the movement of a shadow.

keyWords.example: Our teacher turned the hourglass, and we had until the sand ran out.

keyWords.definition: a wheel with teeth that turns another wheel
keyWords.example: The bicycle chain moves around a gear.

keyWords.definition: one of the tiny parts that everything is made of
keyWords.example: An atom is far too small to see, even with a strong magnifying glass.

How to make a phone at home with tools

wrong.B: The article does not teach how to read a clock.
wrong.C: Egypt is mentioned only for its sundials.
wrong.D: Phones are mentioned at the end, but making them is not the topic.

Sand falls into a glass.
Water drips out of a pot.
The Sun makes a stick cast a shadow that moves.

wrong.A: The article does not mention bells.
wrong.B: That is how an hourglass works.
wrong.C: That is how a water clock works.

A water clock shaped like an elephant

A ship with an hourglass

wrong.C: Sundials in Egypt were used long before al-Jazari.
wrong.D: Sailors used hourglasses, but al-Jazari built a water clock.

questions.stem: Why did people need clocks that did not use the Sun?
options: The Sun moved too fast.
Sundials were much too heavy for people to carry around.
Sundials did not work at night or on cloudy days.
People did not like shadows.
questions.why: Because a sundial needs sunlight, it could not tell time at night or on gray days, so people made other clocks.

checklist: I described how both clocks worked.

MID.modelAnswer: The sundial told time by using a stick that cast a shadow onto marked hours as the Sun moved across the sky. Centuries later, people invented mechanical clocks that used gears to turn the hands, and these worked even at night, unlike the sundial. The mechanical clock was an improvement because it did not depend on sunlight at all, even though early versions were not yet very accurate.

HIGH.prompt: Which invention in the article do you think was the most important step in the history of timekeeping? Defend your choice with evidence from the text.
checklist: I chose one invention and stated my claim clearly.
I compared it with at least one earlier method.
I used evidence and key words from the article.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I think Huygens's pendulum clock was the most important step in the history of timekeeping, because it was the first invention to make timekeeping truly precise. Earlier mechanical clocks used only gears and often lost many minutes every day, but a pendulum swings back and forth at a steady speed, which an engineer could use to regulate a clock far more reliably. This leap in accuracy eventually made it possible to build devices like quartz watches, whose crystals vibrate at a dependable rate, and even atomic clocks, which synchronize to the tiny movements of atoms. Without the pendulum proving that steady, repeating motion could measure time so exactly, modern timekeeping might have developed very differently.
